newsitem.title: CHINA: China cracks down on explosives after bomb blasts.
newsitem.headline: China cracks down on explosives after bomb blasts.

text.p: China on Thursday ordered tighter controls on explosives two days after time-bombs exploded in the restive Moslem region of Xinjiang, killing four people.
A circular from the Ministry of Public Security printed in the People's Daily said illegal explosives were flooding the country and controls were sometimes chaotic.
The statement did not refer to Tuesday's Xinjiang bomb blasts, which official media have ignored.
"Illegally produced dynamite or that stolen from units that have permits to keep explosives are sometimes used by criminals, greatly endangering public safety," it said.

Residents in the Xinjiang capital Urumqi, where three bombs planted on buses blew up within minutes of each other on Tuesday in an apparently coordinated attack, said local authorities had circulated a statement confirming that four people had died.
The statement, which was not issued to the public, ordered tighter security measures, including searches of people and their hand-carried belongings.
"No armed soldiers are seen on the streets now, only more police and teams of security guards are on patrol," one resident said by telephone.
"Policemen are still stationed at almost all bus stops to check suspicious people and their bags," the resident said.
People were still nervous, the resident indicated. "The first thing people say when they call their friends is 'Are you safe and in good health?'"
The blasts, which officials said injured at least 60, occurred within minutes in separate parts of the city, which is the centre of Chinese control over the region and its ethnic Uighur population.

The Ministry of Public Security circular called for tighter supervision of explosives, particularly in rural areas where home-made explosives are often produced for use in small mines and quarries and frequently cause accidents.

Tuesday's explosions in Xinjiang occurred as final rites were being observed in Beijing for Deng Xiaoping, the paramount leader who enforced the integrity of China against separatist threats. He died on February 19.
The bombs were the first known violence in Xinjiang -- a region that Moslem separatists call East Turkestan -- since anti-Chinese riots in Yining on February 5 and 6 left nine people dead.
No one has claimed responsibility for Tuesday's blasts.
Xinjiang, bordering Afghanistan, Pakistan and three mostly-Moslem Central Asian states, was shaken last year by attacks on officials and Moslem leaders regarded as pro-Beijing.
